name: Distributed-ledger family: blockchain-based and ledger-anchored DPPs
scope_note: Covers DPP designs that use a distributed ledger as a store, an integrity anchor, an identity registry, or an access-control and lifecycle engine: permissioned ledgers (Hyperledger Fabric, Besu and GoQuorum consortia), public chains (Ethereum and EVM chains such as Polygon; for Algorand only a non-DPP traceability prototype was located), IOTA (MoveVM objects, notarization, IOTA Identity), and EBSI (Timestamp and Track and Trace services). Records seven design patterns (full data on chain, hash anchoring of an off-chain document, content-addressed storage referenced from chain, token per product, smart-contract lifecycle state machine, confidential or selective disclosure, oracles), the EU legal position, evaluation figures reported in papers, and what a black-box conformance test can verify offline versus with a live node. Leaves out: verifiable-credential mechanics that do not depend on a ledger (method m05), GS1 resolver mechanics (web-resolver family), AAS and dataspace transport, and any content of EN, ISO, IEC, ETSI EN or DIN documents (bibliographic metadata only). Vendor statements are recorded as secondary_only. No live node, wallet, gateway, registry or EBSI endpoint was contacted; only documentation pages, specifications, source code and papers were read.
summary: A ledger-based DPP splits a passport into a small trust anchor on a shared ledger and, in almost all practical designs, a larger document held off chain. The economic operator (or a service provider) serialises the passport, computes a digest, and writes the digest, a pointer, or both into a ledger transaction or smart-contract state; the ledger then provides ordering, a block time, and tamper evidence for that digest. Five storage variants recur: full passport data on chain (rare, costly), a hash imprint of an off-chain document (EBSI Timestamp, Arianee imprint, Fabric private-data hashes), an IPFS content identifier whose multihash is itself the integrity check, a non-fungible token per product item whose tokenURI points to metadata, and a consortium ledger whose chaincode holds structured product records. Smart contracts add a lifecycle state machine (mint or create, update, transfer custody, destroy or deactivate) and on-ledger access rules such as whitelisted issuer DIDs, per-document write and delegate permissions, or federated authority hierarchies. Confidential data stays off chain, inside private data collections, or behind zero-knowledge proofs and selective disclosure; the EDPB guidelines of 2026 advise against plain personal data on chain and describe erasure by deleting off-chain data, salts or keys. A verifier checks integrity by re-hashing the retrieved document and comparing it with the anchored value, then checking that the anchoring transaction is included in a final block of the expected chain; inclusion can be shown offline with a portable proof (OpenTimestamps receipts to a Bitcoin block header, IOTA Proof of Inclusion against a trusted committee, EIP-1186 Merkle proofs against a state root) when the verifier pins a trusted root. Current state, such as the latest tokenURI, the owner, or a revocation flag, needs a live ledger read. EU law is technology-neutral here: the ESPR and the Batteries Regulation ask for a decentralised data system run by economic operators, open interoperable formats, a back-up copy at a DPP service provider and a central Commission registry, but name no ledger; eIDAS 2 gives qualified electronic ledgers a legal presumption of ordering and integrity. The academic literature is dominated by prototypes and conceptual frameworks; reported performance ranges from single-digit transactions per second on public EVM chains to above one thousand on tuned Fabric clusters, and reviews flag cost, scalability, governance, interoperability and GDPR tension as the main problems. For the conformance engine, the anchor-hash comparison and pinned-root inclusion proofs are deterministic offline checks; ledger state queries require a new, explicitly allowlisted ledger-read transport.

maturity.spec_status: No DPP-specific ledger specification exists in EU law or in an open specification read in this session. The building blocks are mature and openly specified: ERC-721, ERC-1155 and ERC-4906 are Final Ethereum standards; CAIP-2 chain identifiers are Final; the IPFS CID specification is marked Permanent; W3C DID 1.1 is a Candidate Recommendation Snapshot (5 March 2026). Some pieces are weaker: EIP-1186 (eth_getProof) is Stagnant; the Ethereum execution-apis JSON-RPC specification is at v1.0.0-beta.7; EBSI service APIs are versioned with a non-backward-compatible version in test; the IOTA Notarization Toolkit is pre-1.0 (v0.1.27; Proof of Inclusion poi-v0.1.0).

maturity.adoption_evidence: Academic: reviews report blockchain as the most frequently proposed DPP enabler but with limited empirical validation and a drift to hybrid architectures (10.1007/s43615-026-00927-x, 225 studies; 10.3390/digital6020043; 10.1016/j.spc.2025.01.014 found blockchain the most adopted security solution among 25 frameworks). Prototypes exist on Hyperledger Fabric, Ethereum and Polygon, GoQuorum, Waves, IOTA, Secret Network and EBSI (see literature). Public pilots: TRACE4EU battery materials traceability on EBSI (official EBSI page; page contains unfinished placeholder text), the IOTA DPP demonstrator (its README states it is a reference showcase and not a regulation-compliant DPP), and the EU Blockchain Observatory and Forum report of 3 May 2024 that interviews Circularise, Circulor, Spherity, nChain, IOTA and DYNE. Commercial: Arianee publishes ERC-721 passport contracts under MIT; Circularise and Minespider describe blockchain-based passports in marketing material only (secondary_only). No production deployment of a ledger-based DPP for a product group regulated by an ESPR delegated act was located; no ESPR delegated act requiring a DPP was located as adopted in the prior record.
maturity.regulatory_alignment: Neutral to permissive; never required. Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, recital 41, says the DPP should rest on a decentralised data system set up and managed by economic operators, with a Commission registry that stores unique identifiers; recital 42 links the Commission web portal to data held in the operator's decentralised DPP. No recital or article read names blockchain, ledger or any storage technology (recitals 1 to 122 and Arts 1 to 26 scanned this session). Art. 10(1)(d) requires open standards, interoperable formats and transfer without vendor lock-in, which constrains proprietary chains. Art. 10(4) (and Art. 27(1)(c), prior record) require a back-up copy through a DPP service provider; Art. 11 points (c), (d), (e), (g), (h) require storage by the operator or service providers, linking a new DPP to the original, availability after insolvency, liquidation or cessation of Union activity, data authentication, reliability and integrity, and high security and privacy with fraud avoidance. Art. 13 has the Commission run a central registry of unique identifiers; it is not described as a ledger. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, recital 126, likewise asks for a decentralised data system maintained by economic operators and names no technology. Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 inserts electronic ledgers as a trust service into Regulation (EU) No 910/2014: Art. 3(52) and (53) define electronic and qualified electronic ledgers, Art. 45k gives ledgers non-discrimination as evidence and a presumption of unique chronological ordering and integrity for qualified ones, and Art. 45l(1)(a)-(d) sets the qualified-ledger requirements; recital 68 asks for technological neutrality between centralised and distributed ledgers; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2531 lists the reference standards that give qualified ledgers a presumption of compliance. Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, Art. 36, applies only where a smart contract executes a data-sharing agreement: it requires robustness and access control, safe termination and interruption, archiving of transaction data and code, governance-layer access control, and consistency with the agreement, plus an EU declaration of conformity. GDPR obligations apply in full; the EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 v2 favour permissioned ledgers and off-chain storage of personal data. ESPR Art. 10(1)(e) bars customer personal data in the DPP without explicit consent, which reduces but does not remove the GDPR tension.

L01_unique_identifiers.mechanism: Ledgers add identifiers of their own; they do not replace the persistent unique product identifier that the law requires. Four ledger-native identifier kinds recur. (1) Token reference: a chain identifier in CAIP-2 form namespace:reference (for example eip155:1 for Ethereum mainnet; namespace [-a-z0-9]{3,8}, reference [-_a-zA-Z0-9]{1,32}, case-sensitive), plus a 20-byte contract address, plus a uint256 tokenId (ERC-721) or token type id (ERC-1155; a type with supply 1 is non-fungible; the optional split-ID scheme puts the set in high bits and the item in low bits). (2) Decentralized identifiers for operators, issuers, and sometimes product items: did:method:method-specific-id per W3C DID 1.1; did:iota:<8-hex network id>:0x<64 hex object id>, mainnet network id 6364aad5 may be omitted; did:ebsi for EBSI legal entities (did:ebsi:z<base58btc of version byte 1 plus 16 random bytes>, network segment omitted on the EBSI chain, resolved through the EBSI DID Registry with an optional valid-at time; new-ebsi-did-method); did:ethr resolved from Ethereum addresses. (3) Content identifiers for documents (not products): CIDv1 = varint version 0x01, content-type multicodec, multihash; text form = multibase prefix plus encoding (b = base32, z = base58btc, f = base16, k = base36); CIDv0 = bare 34-byte sha2-256 multihash (0x12 0x20...), shown as 46-character Qm... base58btc. (4) Hash-derived record identifiers: EBSI Track and Trace documents are identified by an id derived from a hash of their content; an EBSI timestampId is computed locally as the multibase base64url encoding of the multihash of the SHA-256 of the anchored hash. Prototypes also map a GS1 or vendor serial to a tokenId inside the contract, or mint a DID per product (cheqd in 10.3390/app14114874).

L01_unique_identifiers.observable_black_box: Identifier strings in the carrier payload, in the resolved passport and in anchor receipts can be parsed offline: CAIP-2 regex, 0x-prefixed 20-byte address, decimal or hex tokenId, DID syntax and method-specific syntax, CID decode rules (34-byte 0x12 0x20 check, version varint, trailing-byte rejection). Agreement between the carrier identifier, the passport id and the ledger reference is observable without a node when the passport carries the reference; ownership or existence of the token on chain needs a live read.
L01_unique_identifiers.law_delta: ESPR Art. 10(1)(a)-(c) requires a persistent unique product identifier connected through a data carrier and compliant with Annex III standards or harmonised standards. Token ids, contract addresses and DIDs are not identifiers of that kind; a ledger DPP must still carry a compliant product identifier and map it to the ledger reference. A token burned or a contract self-destructed or upgraded can break persistence of the ledger reference, which law does not address.

L02_data_carriers.mechanism: The ledger does not change the physical carrier. The carrier holds a URL (typically a GS1 Digital Link or an operator URL) that resolves to a web page or API, which in turn exposes or embeds the ledger reference; some prototypes encode a tokenId, DID or transaction hash directly in the QR payload. One automotive prototype uses a lazy-minted ERC-721 on Polygon that is minted only when the customer redeems it through a passkey flow (10.1109/compsac69091.2026.00308). No ledger-specific carrier specification was found.

L02_data_carriers.observable_black_box: Decoded carrier payload; whether it is an HTTPS URL or a bare ledger reference; whether a bare ledger reference can be resolved without a wallet. Existing carrier.qr_decode and identifier.parse cover only the GS1 /01/<GTIN>/21/<serial> form.
L02_data_carriers.law_delta: Law requires a carrier that connects to the persistent unique product identifier; a QR that holds only a wallet deep link or a chain reference, without a compliant identifier, would not meet Art. 10(1) as summarised. unknown for product-specific carrier rules (set by delegated acts).

L03_data_exchange_protocols.mechanism: Reads and writes use ledger-specific protocols next to ordinary HTTPS. Ethereum family: JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP POST with Content-Type application/json; methods eth_getTransactionReceipt (fields include blockHash, blockNumber, logs, status 0x1 for success, transactionHash), eth_getTransactionByHash, eth_call for contract views such as tokenURI or tokenImprint, eth_getLogs for events, eth_getProof (EIP-1186, address, storage keys, block) returning accountProof and storageProof as RLP-encoded Merkle Patricia Trie nodes; block parameter tags earliest, finalized, safe, latest, pending, where finalized means crypto-economically secure and latest can be re-orged. Writes are raw signed transactions (eth_sendRawTransaction). EBSI: REST reads such as GET /v1/timestamp/timestamps/{timestampId} and /v1/timestamp/records/{recordId}[/versions[/{versionId}]]; writes are built by the service (methods timestampHashes, timestampRecordHashes, timestampRecordVersionHashes, appendRecordVersionHashes), signed by the client and submitted (eth_sendRawTransaction per the guide), after obtaining an access token with scope 'openid timestamp:write' by presenting a verifiable presentation to a DCQL query; Track and Trace exposes list/get documents, events, accesses, contract details and ABI. IPFS: GET /ipfs/{cid} on a trustless gateway with Accept application/vnd.ipld.raw (single block) or application/vnd.ipld.car (CAR stream), or format=raw|car (format wins over Accept); IPNS records as application/vnd.ipfs.ipns-record. IOTA: gRPC ledger requests by the Proof of Inclusion source; resolvers query objects through an indexer node. Fabric: Gateway API with endorsement, ordering, validation and commit notification (10.1109/access.2025.3650525); private data travels peer-to-peer by gossip.

L03_data_exchange_protocols.law_delta: ESPR Art. 10(1)(d) requires transfer through an open interoperable data exchange network without vendor lock-in; a passport readable only through a proprietary chain client or a consortium-internal gRPC endpoint is in tension with that. Law names no protocol.

L04_apis_lifecycle_searchability.mechanism: Lifecycle operations map onto contract or service calls rather than onto a DPP API. Create: mint (ERC-721 Transfer from the zero address; ERC-1155 TransferSingle with zero-address sender), Arianee reserveToken then hydrateToken(tokenId, bytes32 imprint, uri, ...), EBSI createDocument or timestampRecordHashes, IOTA single notarization or audit-trail creation, Fabric chaincode create. Read: tokenURI(tokenId), uri(id) with {id} replaced by the 64-character lowercase hex id, ownerOf, tokenImprint(tokenId), EBSI GET timestamps or records, IOTA object reads. Update: updateTokenURI (issuer only in Arianee), new metadata behind an unchanged URI signalled by ERC-4906 MetadataUpdate or BatchMetadataUpdate, EBSI timestampRecordVersionHashes or appendRecordVersionHashes, Track and Trace events written to a document. Deactivate: burn (Transfer to zero address) or destroy, EBSI record revocation status, did:iota deactivation (empty document or deactivated flag) or deletion (deleted_did flag, irreversible). Search: event log filtering (eth_getLogs), EBSI list documents, list events, list accesses; no standard query by product attributes. EBSI Track and Trace REST shapes per the create guide: HEAD /v1/track-and-trace/accesses?creator={did} returns 204 when the DID may create documents and 404 otherwise; GET /v1/track-and-trace/documents/{documentId}, .../accesses and .../events read state; writes need scope openid track-and-trace:create or :write and call createDocument, grantAccess or writeEvent, submitted by eth_sendRawTransaction (new-ebsi-create-tnt-doc).

L05_system_interoperability_data_models.mechanism: On-chain state is minimal and technology-specific: a bytes32 imprint and a URI string per token (Arianee), a hash plus submitter, block number and block time per timestamp (EBSI), a hash, sender DID, origin, metadata and timestamp per Track and Trace event, a byte-packed DID document with type marker, version and encoding in an IOTA Identity object. Off-chain metadata follows the token standard: ERC-721 metadata JSON (name, description, image) or ERC-1155 metadata JSON (name, decimals, description, image, properties, localization with uri pattern, default and locales). Passport content itself is free-form JSON in most prototypes; some papers model entities (Product, Manufacturer, Supplier, Material) in chaincode (10.3390/app14114874), wrap data as W3C VCs (TRACE4EU battery pilot; 10.1016/j.procs.2026.02.145), use GS1 EPCIS 2.0 events (10.3390/logistics10080177), or AAS submodels exchanged through a Secret Network contract (10.20944/preprints202402.1194.v2). One pipeline maps sensor data to JSON with an LLM before storing it on the Waves chain (10.1016/j.digbus.2026.100167). No common DPP vocabulary is defined on chain.

L05_system_interoperability_data_models.observable_black_box: The off-chain document is a normal JSON (or JSON-LD) artifact and can be schema-checked; the on-chain record shape is fixed by the contract ABI or service API and can be checked against a captured response or ABI file.
L05_system_interoperability_data_models.law_delta: ESPR Art. 10(1)(d) requires open standards and interoperable, machine-readable, structured, searchable data; ERC metadata schemas are open but carry no DPP semantics, so a ledger DPP still needs a DPP data model. Annex III content is set per product group by delegated act.

L06_storage_archiving_persistence.mechanism: Seven storage placements: (a) full data on chain: every node replicates the passport; high cost and size limits (EUBOF report table; gas figures in 10.1109/icces67310.2025.11336296 and 10.1109/blockchain67634.2025.00025, where each extra 32-byte EVM storage slot costs about 20,000 gas); (b) hash imprint on chain and document off chain: integrity is anchored, availability depends on the off-chain host; (c) IPFS or Filecoin content addressing: the CID guarantees integrity of whatever bytes are returned, but availability depends on pinning; (d) Fabric private data collections: actual data in the private state database of authorised peers, its hash on every channel peer's ledger; automatic purge after a configured number of blocks and explicit PurgePrivateData remove the data but leave the hash as evidence; (e) EBSI: the Timestamp service stores only hashes, never the data; (f) IOTA: notarization objects can hold arbitrary data, a document hash, or latest-state records, with locked or dynamic variants; (g) hybrid: critical fields on chain, bulk data off chain. Ledger replication gives durability of the anchor itself, not of the off-chain document. Link rot is a known risk: one study found 45% of ERC-721 tokens in its six-month Ethereum corpus failed a basic permanence criterion (10.48550/arxiv.2209.14517).

L06_storage_archiving_persistence.observable_black_box: Whether the off-chain document is retrievable now; whether retrieved bytes match the anchored hash or CID; whether the passport names a back-up service provider (Annex III point (l) field, when the delegated act requires it). Long-term availability cannot be observed in one run; persistence.scheduled is interface_only.
L06_storage_archiving_persistence.law_delta: ESPR requires availability for at least the expected product lifetime (Art. 9(2)(i)), availability after insolvency (Art. 11(e)), storage by the operator or service providers (Art. 11(c)) and a back-up copy through a DPP service provider (Art. 10(4); recital 38). The text read does not say whether replication on a ledger can serve as that back-up; ledger durability covers only the anchor, not the document. EN 18221 content not used.

L07_access_rights_security_confidentiali.mechanism: Public ledgers expose every transaction to everyone, so confidentiality is built around the ledger: (1) keep restricted data off chain behind an authenticated API and anchor only a salted or keyed hash; (2) permissioned ledgers with channel membership and Fabric private data collections (non-members can read only the hash, via GetPrivateDataHash, and verify data shared out of band); (3) on-ledger permission models: EBSI Track and Trace permissions creator, write and delegate per document, with creators restricted to legal entities whose DID is whitelisted in the DID Registry; IOTA Hierarchies authorisation chain Root of Authority to Manufacturer to Repairer (IOTA DPP demonstrator); Arianee issuer-only updates and hashed access tokens per token; NFT ownership as access right (soulbound ERC-721 in 10.1109/blockchain67634.2025.00025); (4) zero-knowledge proofs: Groth16 proofs over EPCIS sensor predicates with 304 ms mean proving and 9.8 ms verification (10.3390/logistics10080177); wallet, NFT and ZKP textile prototype (10.24251/hicss.2025.527); vendor claims of ZKP-based selective querying (Circularise, secondary_only); (5) multi-party computation and on-premise nodes (Re|Source per EUBOF report). GDPR: EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 v2 discourage plain personal data on chain, treat salted or keyed hashes and encrypted data as still personal data, recommend permissioned designs and a DPIA, and describe erasure by deleting off-chain data, keys or salts; redactable-chain research uses chameleon hashes (10.1109/access.2025.3594656) and dual-layer redaction (10.1109/brains67003.2025.11302930); crypto-shredding audit framework (10.1109/brains67003.2025.11302955).

L08_authentication_reliability_integrity.mechanism: This is the core contribution of the family. Integrity chain for a hash-anchored passport: (1) canonicalise the passport (raw bytes, or JSON canonicalised per RFC 8785 when the design says so) and hash it with a declared algorithm (multihash code, or an algorithm id such as SHA-256; the EBSI create-timestamp guide shows SHA-256 wrapped in a multihash and encoded multibase base64url with prefix u, new-ebsi-create-timestamp); (2) the anchor holds that digest: EBSI timestamp hash, Arianee bytes32 imprint, Fabric private-data hash, IOTA notarization payload, or a Merkle root over a batch (Merkle-tree batching cuts anchoring cost in 10.3390/logistics10080177); (3) the anchor is included in the ledger: a transaction hash in a block of a given chain; on EVM chains the receipt status must be 0x1 and the block should be at or below the finalized tag; EBSI records the block number and block timestamp under Proof of Authority consensus; (4) the anchor's author is authenticated: the transaction sender account, an EBSI whitelisted legal-entity DID, a did:iota controller, or an issuer DID in a VC. Portable inclusion evidence lets a verifier skip a live node: an OpenTimestamps .ots receipt carries the hash path from the document digest to a Bitcoin block header (verification needs the header, from a local node or a pinned copy; pending receipts need a calendar server); an IOTA Proof of Inclusion bundles the transaction, effects, events, user signatures and a checkpoint summary, verified locally against a committee that the caller anchors from a trusted genesis blob or trusted node; an EIP-1186 account and storage proof walks the Merkle Patricia Trie from a trusted block stateRoot to a contract storage slot. Legal trust: qualified electronic ledgers under eIDAS 2 (Art. 45l(1): created and managed by one or more qualified trust service providers, origin of records established, unique sequential chronological order, changes immediately detectable) enjoy a presumption of ordering and integrity (Art. 45k(2)); Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2531 lists the reference standards and, in its annex, asks for record origin through advanced electronic signatures or seals based on qualified certificates, ordering through cryptographic hash links or qualified timestamps, automatic ledger reports, and extra architecture and governance references for DLT-based providers. Credential layer: W3C VCs whose issuer DIDs and status lists are held on EBSI (TRACE4EU) are covered by method m05.

L08_authentication_reliability_integrity.observable_black_box: Offline: recomputed digest of the sample document versus the digest in the receipt; Merkle audit path from digest to batch root; inclusion proof from root to a pinned block header, state root or committee-certified checkpoint; consistency of chain id, transaction hash and block number fields. Live only: that the transaction exists on the canonical chain now, its confirmation depth or finality, and the current contract state.
L08_authentication_reliability_integrity.law_delta: ESPR Art. 11(g) requires data authentication, reliability and integrity without naming a mechanism. A ledger anchor gives tamper evidence and a time order; it does not prove the data were true when written (garbage-in), which reviews and the EUBOF report flag and which oracles or multi-party review only partly address. Only qualified electronic ledgers get the eIDAS 2 legal presumption; an ordinary chain anchor has evidential value but no presumption. EN 18246 content not used.

L09_registry_and_customs.mechanism: The ESPR splits storage (decentralised, operator-run) from a central Commission registry of unique identifiers that national authorities and customs can access (recitals 41, 42, 44). A ledger DPP does not replace that registry. Art. 13 (re-read this session): the Commission sets up the registry by 19 July 2026; it stores at least the unique identifiers, the commodity code for goods released for free circulation, and battery unique identifiers; delegated acts may add data; operators upload the data; the registry returns a unique registration identifier that is not proof of compliance (13(5)); the Commission, national authorities and customs have access (13(6)). Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1778 (prior record, not re-read) has verified operators register passports through a user interface or API, receive a persistent registration identifier, and can obtain a proof of registration with a Commission timestamp, a hash and a qualified electronic seal; changes are logged and versioned with Commission timestamps. Nothing read says that the registry uses a distributed ledger. EBSI is an EU-level ledger infrastructure, but no source read links it to the DPP registry.

L10_lifecycle_versioning_updates.mechanism: Versioning is append-only by construction: EBSI Timestamp records hold an ordered sequence of version hashes with owners and a revocation status; Track and Trace events cannot be modified or deleted after writing; IOTA audit trails hold sequential entries with role-based access, locking and tagging; Fabric keeps history even after DelPrivateData, and PurgePrivateData leaves the hash. Token designs differ: ERC-721 allows tokenURI to be mutable (rationale section), so a metadata change can happen without a new on-chain record unless the contract implements ERC-4906, which then MUST emit MetadataUpdate or BatchMetadataUpdate when the JSON metadata changes (the event carries no metadata). Arianee lets the issuer change the URI (updateTokenURI) and keeps one imprint per token. Handover between operators maps to token transfer (Transfer event), to EBSI grant of write or delegate access, or to a new controller of a did:iota identity (threshold voting). Deactivation and end of life: burn to the zero address, destroy, EBSI record revocation, did:iota deactivation or irreversible deletion; the IOTA Identity object persists after its DID is deleted. Smart-contract state machines encode statuses such as PRODUCED, SHIPPED, RECEIVED BY RETAILER, SOLD, RECYCLED (ChromaWay example in the EUBOF report) or the Batteries Regulation status values.

L10_lifecycle_versioning_updates.law_delta: ESPR requires data to be up to date (Art. 9(1)), a new DPP for a product that already has one to be linked to the original (Art. 11(d)) and availability for the set period (Art. 11(e)). Immutability is not a legal requirement; the EUBOF report notes that immutability is not a prerequisite of the EU DPP. A burn or delete on chain must not make the passport unavailable before the retention period ends.

L11_roles_and_governance.mechanism: Governance models: (1) private consortium ledgers (Fabric, Besu with QBFT, GoQuorum) where members run nodes and admit participants; a national Besu rootchain reached about 800 write transactions per second with p99 finality under 3 s on 5 to 14 validators (10.1109/access.2026.3726043); (2) public permissionless chains (Ethereum, Polygon, Bitcoin via OpenTimestamps) where anyone validates and writers pay fees; (3) public permissioned infrastructure run by public bodies (EBSI: Proof of Authority, creators whitelisted by an authorised authority or the support office); (4) DAG ledgers with sponsored fees (IOTA Gas Station in the demonstrator) and federated authority hierarchies; (5) trust frameworks over the ledger: DIDs and VCs, Root of Authority accreditation, multi-signature reviewers and oracles (EUBOF table). Legal roles: the EDPB treats nodes on permissionless chains as possible controllers or joint controllers and encourages a consortium or legal entity to take that role; eIDAS 2 makes qualified trust service providers responsible for qualified ledgers; Data Act Art. 36 places conformity duties on vendors or deployers of smart contracts that execute data-sharing agreements; ESPR service providers may not reuse DPP data beyond the service (Art. 11, second subparagraph).

end_to_end_flows.name: Hash-anchored off-chain passport on EBSI Timestamp
actors: EBSI Ledger service and Timestamp contract
steps: 1. The operator serialises the passport document and computes its digest with the algorithm it declares.
2. The operator obtains an access token with scope openid timestamp:write by answering a DCQL query with a verifiable presentation.

3. The operator asks the Timestamp API to build a transaction (timestampHashes, or timestampRecordHashes for a versioned record), signs it locally and submits it (eth_sendRawTransaction per the guide).
4. The contract records the hash, the submitting account, the block number and the block timestamp; the data itself is never sent.
5. The operator publishes the passport at its own host and states the timestampId (multibase base64url of the multihash of SHA-256 of the hash) or record id in the passport or its metadata.
6. For an update, the operator adds a version with timestampRecordVersionHashes or appendRecordVersionHashes.
7. The verifier fetches the passport, recomputes the digest, derives the timestampId and reads GET /v1/timestamp/timestamps/{timestampId}, then compares hash, timestampedBy and block data.

end_to_end_flows.name: Token-per-product passport with hash imprint (ERC-721)
steps: 1. The issuer reserves a tokenId and hydrates it with a bytes32 imprint of the passport JSON, a URI, and access keys.
2. The passport JSON is hosted off chain at the URI; private parts sit behind a gateway that checks hashed access rights.
3. Custody changes are ERC-721 transfers; Transfer events form the ownership history.
4. The issuer can change the URI (updateTokenURI); a contract that implements ERC-4906 must emit MetadataUpdate when the JSON changes.
5. A verifier reads tokenURI and tokenImprint for the tokenId on the declared chain, downloads the JSON, hashes it and compares it with the imprint.
6. End of life uses destroy or burn; the passport document should remain available for the retention period.

end_to_end_flows.name: CID-referenced passport (IPFS plus on-chain pointer)
steps: 1. The operator adds the passport (or a DAG of files) to IPFS and obtains a CIDv1.
2. The CID is written to chain, in a token URI (ipfs://<cid>) or in contract storage; content-addressed storage needs active pinning to stay available.
3. The verifier requests GET /ipfs/{cid}?format=raw (or car) from any gateway.
4. The verifier hashes each received block and checks that the digest equals the CID multihash; a CAR stream must be complete.
5. An update produces a new CID; the on-chain pointer changes and, for ERC-721 with ERC-4906, an update event is emitted.

end_to_end_flows.name: Consortium ledger with private data (Hyperledger Fabric)
steps: 1. A member submits a chaincode transaction; restricted fields go into a private data collection.
2. Authorised peers store the private data and gossip it; the hash of the private data is ordered and written to every channel peer's ledger.
3. Other members query public chaincode state; a non-member receives private data out of band and checks it against the on-chain hash via GetPrivateDataHash.
4. Private data is purged after the configured block count or by PurgePrivateData; the hash stays as evidence.

end_to_end_flows.name: Offline verification of an anchor receipt with a portable inclusion proof
actors: trust-root custodian (pinned headers, genesis blob, or committee)
steps: 1. The SUT supplies a sample bundle: the passport bytes, an anchor receipt (digest, algorithm, chain id, transaction or checkpoint reference) and an inclusion proof (.ots file, IOTA PoI proof, or EIP-1186 proof plus block header).
2. The engine recomputes the digest from the passport bytes and compares it with the receipt.
3. The engine verifies the Merkle path from the digest (or batch leaf) to the root committed in the block header, state root or certified checkpoint.
4. The engine authenticates the header, state root or checkpoint against a trust root pinned in the test pack (Bitcoin headers, IOTA genesis-derived committee, Ethereum finalized header).
5. The engine reports digest match, path validity and root trust as separate findings; anything that needs current chain state is reported as not run.

end_to_end_flows.name: Credential-centred battery passport anchored on EBSI (TRACE4EU pilot)
steps: 1. An audit firm issues a product-carbon-footprint verifiable credential; a certification body issues responsible-mining credentials; participants hold legal-identity and Catena-X membership credentials.
2. The manufacturer issues a Battery Passport credential tied to the serial number that links to the PCF credential, a due diligence report, and an access point for confidential data.
3. Verifiers check issuer credentials against the EBSI ledger; a consumer scans the serial number to view and verify the passport.

failure_modes.fault: The anchor hash is computed over a non-canonical JSON serialisation, so a semantically identical re-served document no longer matches.
failure_modes.detectable_by: integrity.anchor_hash with a reordered-key fixture and the receipt's declared canonicalisation.

failure_modes.fault: The receipt names no hash algorithm or a multihash code that does not match the digest length.
failure_modes.detectable_by: Receipt parsing in integrity.anchor_hash; multihash length check.

failure_modes.fault: The receipt points to a reverted transaction (status 0x0) or a block that was re-orged out.
failure_modes.detectable_by: ledger.read against a mock or live node; finalized tag comparison.

failure_modes.fault: An inclusion proof verifies against a root that the verifier never authenticated (for example a self-supplied block header).
failure_modes.detectable_by: integrity.inclusion_proof requires a pinned trust root and reports root trust as a separate finding.

failure_modes.fault: A CID string fails CIDv0 or CIDv1 decoding (wrong multibase, trailing bytes, reserved version).
failure_modes.detectable_by: identifier.ledger_ref decode rules from the IPFS CID specification.

failure_modes.fault: The receipt states a bare numeric chain id or a chain name instead of a namespaced chain id, so the anchor is ambiguous across chains.
The off-chain document behind an anchor or CID is no longer pinned or hosted (link rot).
failure_modes.detectable_by: Retrieval failure in identifier.resolve or storage.cid_verify; repeated over time needs persistence.scheduled (interface_only).

failure_modes.fault: A gateway returns bytes that do not hash to the requested CID.
tokenURI or the JSON behind it changes without a MetadataUpdate event although the contract claims ERC-4906.
failure_modes.detectable_by: ledger.events on captured logs plus supportsInterface(0x49064906).

failure_modes.fault: The token is burned or destroyed and the resolver drops the passport before the retention period ends, or keeps serving it with no deactivated marker.
failure_modes.detectable_by: lifecycle.deactivation on a loopback SUT; identifier.resolve availability.

failure_modes.fault: A version is silently replaced instead of appended (mutable pointer with no history).
failure_modes.detectable_by: persistence.versions comparing successive captures; per-version hash checks.

failure_modes.fault: Restricted or personal data is written in clear to calldata, event data or public token metadata.
failure_modes.detectable_by: access.onchain_leak canary search on captured payloads.

failure_modes.fault: An unsalted hash of a low-entropy personal field is anchored on a public chain, which allows dictionary reversal.
failure_modes.detectable_by: access.onchain_leak dictionary test over declared low-entropy fields.

failure_modes.fault: After an erasure request the off-chain endpoint still returns the record (200) while the operator claims erasure.
The issuer DID (for example did:iota with deleted_did set, or a deactivated document) is still presented as a live issuer.
failure_modes.detectable_by: integrity.issuer_binding against a pinned DID document with the deletion flag.

failure_modes.fault: The anchor was written by a key not bound to the declared economic operator.
failure_modes.detectable_by: integrity.issuer_binding comparison of sender key and pinned DID document.

failure_modes.fault: The passport is only readable through a proprietary chain client or wallet, with no open HTTP read path.
failure_modes.detectable_by: identifier.resolve fails to reach a JSON passport from the carrier payload; manual.review of the ICS.

failure_modes.fault: An anchor receipt gives a raw hex SHA-256 digest where the ledger stores a multibase base64url multihash (or the reverse), so a correct document fails comparison or a wrong one is compared against the wrong bytes.
failure_modes.detectable_by: integrity.anchor_hash decodes the declared encoding, checks the multihash code and length, and reports an encoding mismatch separately from a digest mismatch.

open_questions: Can replication on a distributed ledger, or a ledger operated by a DPP service provider, satisfy the ESPR Art. 10(4) back-up copy duty? The texts read do not say; the Art. 11 delegated act on service providers is not adopted (prior record).
Will product delegated acts or the Art. 11 service-provider act mention ledgers, anchoring or qualified electronic ledgers at all? Nothing located.
Does the EU DPP registry (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1778) use any ledger for its timestamps or logs? Not stated in the prior summary; not re-read.

Contract change needed in the engine: section 9 transport policy has no notion of a read-only ledger endpoint (JSON-RPC node, IPFS gateway, EBSI read API). A ledger.read capability needs an allowlist, a pinned chain id, a finality rule, and recording of responses for replay. Report to the owner; do not edit architecture.md.
How should ICS and IXIT express a chain-qualified anchor (chain id, contract, token or record id, algorithm, canonicalisation) and the pinned trust root for inclusion proofs?

Should the engine accept EIP-1186 proofs as evidence given the EIP is Stagnant? The maintained execution-apis specification does carry eth_getProof (src/eth/state.yaml), so the response shape is specified; the owner should decide which reference the oracle cites.

Would an operator that anchors on a qualified electronic ledger (eIDAS 2, Art. 45l; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2531) gain any presumption relevant to ESPR Art. 11(g)? No link between the two regimes was found in the texts read.
The EUBOF report states that the Battery Pass platform relies on a private permissioned blockchain; this was not checked against the Battery Pass technical guidance and may be a mischaracterisation.

Partly resolved 2026-10-19: the EBSI create-timestamp guide shows SHA-256 digests as multihash in multibase base64url (prefix u). Still open: whether the Timestamp API accepts other multihash codes, and how Track and Trace derives documentId (the create-tnt-doc guide does not say).
